steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting Spyx, a JAX-based library for just-in-time compiled training of spiking neural networks. Motivate neuromorphic computing, survey existing SNN training libraries including the recent JAX-based ones, and position Spyx and the paper's performance comparison.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Hardware lottery and energy cost of deep learning; neuromorphic computing and SNNs as an answer
- Heterogeneous neuromorphic hardware -> GPU-based, platform-agnostic training
- Existing SNN training libraries: low-level, high-level, platform-specific
- JAX and its ecosystem
- JAX-based SNN work
- Spyx and what this paper does

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - since "Attention is All You Need" (cite): capacity/capability of AI accelerators exploded
  - "Hardware Lottery" (cite): training massive DNNs drives investment in parallel, dense matrix hardware -> more DNN performance
  - dramatic energy and environmental cost of training/deploying (cite)
  - neuromorphic computing + SNNs: inspired by biology; sparsity, event-based computation, low-power custom hardware
- Hardware ecosystem
  - heterogeneous, experimental; on-chip learning hard/impossible to transfer between platforms
  - frameworks in last five years: GPU-based training/simulation of platform-agnostic SNNs, then conversion/transfer to target device
- Libraries (direct training only; ANN-to-SNN conversion not a focus)
  - high-power training for low-power; each library different tradeoffs
  - custom low-level: mlGeNN (custom CUDA kernels) (cite), SpikingJelly (PyTorch + custom CUDA) (cite): speed vs flexibility/interoperability
  - higher-level: snnTorch (cite), Norse (cite): extend PyTorch, simpler programming, less hardware optimization (dynamic graphs); less of a drawback for multi-node or very large datasets
  - platform-specific: Lava-dl (cite) for Intel's Loihi (cite); Rockpool (cite) for SynSense's Xylo (cite)
- JAX
  - 2023: SNN research powered by JAX (cite), Google DeepMind
  - JIT compilation for AI accelerators, composable function transformations (vectorization), automatic differentiation
  - Numpy-like, functional -> ecosystem: differentiable physics simulator (cite), RL environments (cite), evolutionary optimization tools (cite)
- JAX-based SNN work
  - Finkbeiner et al. (cite): sparse vector computation, NVIDIA GPUs vs Graphcore IPUs; MIMD vs SIMD; significant acceleration on IPU
  - Jaxsnn (cite): continuous-time, like ml-GeN (cite) and Norse (cite), no fixed time grid; event-based training; time-to-first-spike (cite), EventProp (cite); BrainScaleS-2 integration (cite)
- Spyx
  - concurrent with other JAX work, inspired by snnTorch (cite); Spyx (cite) for modern evolutionary strategies for SNNs (cite)
  - flexibility of PyTorch frameworks + performance of low-level kernel libraries
  - custom surrogate gradients / neuron models in a few lines; whole training/evaluation loop traced and executed on GPU or TPU at maximum utilization
  - this paper: simulation performance comparison vs other SNN libraries; source on GitHub, releases on PyPI (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Since the publication of "Attention is All You Need" started an avalanche of research into transformer neural network architectures, the capacity and capability of modern AI accelerators has exploded. A direct result is a self-reinforcing cycle that has been called the "Hardware Lottery". The demand to train more and more massive deep neural networks drives a lot of investment in AI hardware, and this hardware prioritizes parallel and dense matrix computations, which then make even greater DNN performance possible. A big concern with the current trajectory of deep learning research and industrial adoption is that training and deploying these models has an equally dramatic energy and environmental cost. The field of neuromorphic computing and the investigation of Spiking Neural Network architectures take inspiration from biology and aim to drastically reduce the computational resources that ML tools need, by using sparsity and event-based computation executed on low-power custom hardware.

The neuromorphic hardware ecosystem has highly heterogeneous architectures and is experimental, and this creates unique challenges for developing SNN models, because on-chip learning for one platform can be difficult or impossible to transfer to other systems. So a number of neuromorphic frameworks developed in the last five years have instead chosen to use the immense support for GPU-based development, so that platform-agnostic SNNs can be trained and simulated on high-performance hardware before they are converted and transferred to a specific target device.

Almost all SNN training frameworks share the motivation of high-power training for low-power, but each library goes about it differently, with its own advantages and drawbacks. Here we focus on libraries for direct training of SNNs. The other popular approach, converting a trained artificial neural network to an SNN, also follows the high-to-low power paradigm but it is not a focus of this paper. Some libraries use custom low-level code. For example, mlGeNN is built on custom low-level CUDA kernels that implement the neuron dynamics, and SpikingJelly builds on PyTorch but adds custom CUDA, which improves computational speed with some tradeoffs in flexibility and interoperability. Higher-level frameworks like snnTorch and Norse instead promote flexibility by extending the PyTorch deep learning framework without adding low-level code. This gives a simpler programming experience, but hardware optimization suffers because of dynamic computation graphs, though this drawback is less significant for multi-node training or if the dataset is extremely large. Finally, some libraries like Lava-dl and Rockpool offer tooling, features, and abstraction models targeted at their own neuromorphic computing platforms, which are Intel's Loihi and SynSense's Xylo hardware families respectively.

- JAX
  - 2023: SNN research powered by JAX, developed by Google DeepMind
  - JIT compilation for AI accelerators, composable transformations (vectorization), automatic differentiation
  - Numpy-like, functional -> ecosystem: differentiable physics simulator, RL environments, evolutionary optimization tools
- JAX-based SNN work
  - Finkbeiner et al.: NVIDIA GPUs vs Graphcore IPUs, MIMD vs SIMD, IPU much faster for sparse SNN simulation
  - Jaxsnn: continuous-time like ml-GeN and Norse, no fixed time grid; time-to-first-spike, EventProp; BrainScaleS-2
- Spyx
  - inspired by snnTorch; for evolutionary strategies for SNNs
  - PyTorch-style flexibility + low-level-kernel performance; custom surrogate gradients / neuron models; full loop on GPU or TPU
  - this paper: simulation performance comparison; GitHub, PyPI

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Since the publication of "Attention is All You Need" started an avalanche of research into transformer neural network architectures, the capacity and capability of modern AI accelerators has exploded. A direct result is a self-reinforcing cycle that has been called the "Hardware Lottery". The demand to train more and more massive deep neural networks drives a lot of investment in AI hardware, and this hardware prioritizes parallel and dense matrix computations, which then make even greater DNN performance possible. A big concern with the current trajectory of deep learning research and industrial adoption is that training and deploying these models has an equally dramatic energy and environmental cost. The field of neuromorphic computing and the investigation of Spiking Neural Network architectures take inspiration from biology and aim to drastically reduce the computational resources that ML tools need, by using sparsity and event-based computation executed on low-power custom hardware.

The neuromorphic hardware ecosystem has highly heterogeneous architectures and is experimental, and this creates unique challenges for developing SNN models, because on-chip learning for one platform can be difficult or impossible to transfer to other systems. So a number of neuromorphic frameworks developed in the last five years have instead chosen to use the immense support for GPU-based development, so that platform-agnostic SNNs can be trained and simulated on high-performance hardware before they are converted and transferred to a specific target device.

Almost all SNN training frameworks share the motivation of high-power training for low-power, but each library goes about it differently, with its own advantages and drawbacks. Here we focus on libraries for direct training of SNNs. The other popular approach, converting a trained artificial neural network to an SNN, also follows the high-to-low power paradigm but it is not a focus of this paper. Some libraries use custom low-level code. For example, mlGeNN is built on custom low-level CUDA kernels that implement the neuron dynamics, and SpikingJelly builds on PyTorch but adds custom CUDA, which improves computational speed with some tradeoffs in flexibility and interoperability. Higher-level frameworks like snnTorch and Norse instead promote flexibility by extending the PyTorch deep learning framework without adding low-level code. This gives a simpler programming experience, but hardware optimization suffers because of dynamic computation graphs, though this drawback is less significant for multi-node training or if the dataset is extremely large. Finally, some libraries like Lava-dl and Rockpool offer tooling, features, and abstraction models targeted at their own neuromorphic computing platforms, which are Intel's Loihi and SynSense's Xylo hardware families respectively.

In 2023, SNN research powered by JAX emerged. JAX is a new and growing high-performance array computing framework developed by Google DeepMind. It has Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation for execution on AI accelerators, composable function transformations like vectorization, and automatic differentiation. Because it has a Numpy-like interface and follows functional programming paradigms, JAX has a growing community of libraries that connect easily, such as a differentiable physics simulator, reinforcement learning environments, or evolutionary optimization tools.

Again, each approach tackles slightly different issues in training SNNs, this time using the unique features of JAX. Finkbeiner et al. compared the performance of sparse vector computation on NVIDIA GPUs and Graphcore Intelligence Processing Units (IPUs) with a JAX-based implementation. They found significant acceleration for sparse SNN simulation with the IPU's Multiple-Instruction, Multiple-Data (MIMD) architecture compared to the GPU's Single-Instruction, Multiple-Data (SIMD) construction. Jaxsnn, a continuous-time library for SNN simulation, also came out. Like ml-GeN and Norse, it avoids discretizing spiking data into a fixed time grid, which is common in other SNN libraries. Instead Jaxsnn is made for event-based training and supports data-sparse training approaches including time-to-first-spike and EventProp, and it supports hardware integration with the BrainScaleS-2 platform.

At the same time as the other JAX-based SNN work, and inspired by the approach of snnTorch, the Spyx library was developed to make it efficient to investigate modern evolutionary strategies for optimizing SNNs. Spyx combines the flexibility of PyTorch-based frameworks with the performance and efficiency of libraries that are backed by low-level kernel implementations. In particular, with Spyx the user can specify their own surrogate gradient functions or neuron models in only a few lines of code, and the whole training and evaluation loop can be reliably traced and executed on a GPU or a TPU with maximum utilization.

This paper compares the simulation performance of Spyx and other notable SNN libraries that sit at the intersection of deep learning and neuromorphic computing. The source code is on GitHub and the package is regularly released and updated on the Python Package Index (PyPI).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Since the avalanche of research into transformer neural network architectures resulting from the publication of "Attention is All You Need" [1], the capacity and capability of modern AI accelerators has exploded. A direct result of this is a self-reinforcing cycle deemed the "Hardware Lottery" [2], where the demand to train increasingly massive deep neural networks drives tremendous investment in AI hardware that prioritizes parallel and dense matrix computations, which in turn facilitate even greater performance of DNN models. A significant concern with the current trajectory of deep learning research and industrial adoption lies in the equally dramatic energy and environmental cost of training and deploying such models [3]. Taking inspiration from biology, the field of neuromorphic computing and the investigation of Spiking Neural Network architectures aim to drastically reduce the computational resources required by ML tools by leveraging sparsity and event-based computation executed on low-power custom hardware.

The highly heterogeneous architectures and experimental nature of the neuromorphic hardware ecosystem pose unique challenges to developing SNN models, since on-chip learning for one platform may be difficult or impossible to transfer to other systems. Consequently, a number of neuromorphic frameworks developed in the last five years have instead opted to leverage the immense support for GPU-based development, enabling the training and simulation of platform-agnostic SNNs on high-performance hardware before conversion and transfer to a specific target device.

While the motivation of high-power training for low-power underpins almost all SNN training frameworks, each library pursues this objective in a different fashion, with associated advantages and drawbacks. In the following we focus on libraries for direct training of SNNs; the other popular approach of converting a trained artificial neural network to an SNN also adheres to the high-to-low power paradigm but is not a focus of this paper. Some libraries use custom low-level code: for example, mlGeNN [4] is built upon custom low-level CUDA kernels implementing the neuron dynamics, and SpikingJelly [5] builds on PyTorch but augments it with custom CUDA, improving computational speed with some tradeoffs in flexibility and interoperability. In contrast, higher-level frameworks such as snnTorch [6] and Norse [7] promote flexibility by extending the PyTorch deep learning framework without adding low-level code, enabling a simpler programming experience at the cost of hardware optimization due to dynamic computation graphs, though this is a less significant drawback for multi-node training or when the dataset is extremely large. Finally, some libraries such as Lava-dl [8] and Rockpool [9] offer tooling, features, and abstraction models targeted at their specific neuromorphic computing platforms, Intel's Loihi [10] and SynSense's Xylo [9] hardware families respectively.

The year 2023 has seen the emergence of SNN research powered by JAX [11], the new and growing high-performance array computing framework developed by Google DeepMind. JAX features Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation for execution on AI accelerators, composable function transformations like vectorization, and automatic differentiation capabilities. Because of its Numpy-like interface and adherence to functional programming paradigms, JAX hosts a growing community of easily connectable libraries such as a differentiable physics simulator [12], reinforcement learning environments [13,14,15], or evolutionary optimization tools [16].

Continuing the trend, each approach again tackles slightly different issues in training SNNs, this time capitalizing on the unique features of JAX. Finkbeiner et al. [17] compared the performance of sparse vector computation on NVIDIA GPUs against Graphcore Intelligence Processing Units (IPUs) using a JAX-based implementation, finding significant acceleration for sparse SNN simulation when using the IPU's Multiple-Instruction, Multiple-Data (MIMD) architecture instead of the GPU's Single-Instruction, Multiple-Data (SIMD) construction. Jaxsnn [18], a continuous-time library for SNN simulation, also debuted, drawing parallels to ml-GeN [4] and Norse [7] by avoiding the discretization of spiking data into a fixed time grid as is common in other SNN libraries. Instead, Jaxsnn is tailored for event-based training, facilitates data-sparse training approaches including time-to-first-spike [19] and EventProp [20], and supports hardware integration with the BrainScaleS-2 platform [21].

Concurrent with other JAX-based SNN work and inspired by the approach of snnTorch [6], the Spyx [22] library was developed to facilitate the efficient investigation of modern evolutionary strategies for optimizing SNNs [23]. Spyx combines the flexibility of PyTorch-based frameworks with the performance and efficiency of libraries backed by low-level kernel implementations. Specifically, Spyx allows the user to specify their own surrogate gradient functions or neuron models in only a few lines of code, while the entire training and evaluation loop can be reliably traced and executed on either a GPU or TPU with maximum utilization.

This paper presents a comparison of simulation performance between Spyx and other notable SNN libraries which sit at the intersection of deep learning and neuromorphic computing. The source code is located on GitHub, and the package is regularly released and updated on the Python Package Index (PyPI) [24].
